claim: Learning alters cortical representations and improves perception.
source: Learning alters cortical representations and improves perception.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the broader scientific literature and serves as the premise for the study.

claim: Apical tuft dendrites in cortical layer 1 are unique in their connectivity and biophysical properties.
source: Apical tuft dendrites in cortical layer 1, which are unique in their connectivity and biophysical properties, may be a key site of learning-induced plasticity.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about the anatomical and functional properties of apical dendrites.

claim: Apical tuft dendrites may be a key site of learning-induced plasticity.
source: Apical tuft dendrites in cortical layer 1, which are unique in their connectivity and biophysical properties, may be a key site of learning-induced plasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis that motivates the study.

claim: Two-photon and SCAPE microscopy were used to longitudinally track tuft-wide calcium spikes in apical dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons in barrel cortex as mice learned a tactile behavior.
source: We used both two-photon and SCAPE microscopy to longitudinally track tuft-wide calcium spikes in apical dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons in barrel cortex as mice learned a tactile behavior.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Mice were trained to discriminate two orthogonal directions of whisker stimulation.
source: Mice were trained to discriminate two orthogonal directions of whisker stimulation.
evidence: This describes the behavioral paradigm used in the study.

claim: Reinforcement learning enhanced tuft selectivity for both directions equally, even though only one was associated with reward.
source: Reinforcement learning, but not repeated stimulus exposure, enhanced tuft selectivity for both directions equally, even though only one was associated with reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Repeated stimulus exposure did not enhance tuft selectivity.
source: Reinforcement learning, but not repeated stimulus exposure, enhanced tuft selectivity for both directions equally, even though only one was associated with reward.
evidence: This is a finding from the control group in the study.

claim: Selective tufts emerged from initially unresponsive or low-selectivity populations.
source: Selective tufts emerged from initially unresponsive or low-selectivity populations.
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal tracking of individual tufts.

claim: Animal movement and choice did not account for changes in stimulus selectivity.
source: Animal movement and choice did not account for changes in stimulus selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control analyses examining the relationship between behavior and neural activity.

claim: Enhanced selectivity persisted even after rewards were removed and animals ceased performing the task.
source: Enhanced selectivity persisted even after rewards were removed and animals ceased performing the task.
evidence: This is a finding from the post-conditioning session.

claim: Learning produces long-lasting realignment of apical dendrite tuft responses to behaviorally relevant dimensions of a task.
source: We conclude that learning produces long-lasting realignment of apical dendrite tuft responses to behaviorally relevant dimensions of a task.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: As animals learn the behavioral relevance of stimuli in a sensory discrimination task, neural representations of those stimuli are enhanced.
source: For example, as animals learn the behavioral relevance of stimuli in a sensory discrimination task, neural representations of those stimuli are enhanced (Poort et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2020; Henschke et al., 2020; Beitel et al., 2003; Goltstein et al., 2013; David et al., 2012; Fritz et al., 2003), potentially improving the salience of information relayed to downstream areas.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Top-down signals from distant cortical regions can modify sensory representations during learning in primary somatosensory and visual cortex.
source: Studies in primary somatosensory (S1) Banerjee et al., 2020 and visual cortex Liu et al., 2020 have revealed that top-down signals from distant cortical regions can modify sensory representations during learning, although the cellular and circuit mechanisms underlying this plasticity remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: The cellular and circuit mechanisms underlying learning-related plasticity remain unclear.
source: Studies in primary somatosensory (S1) Banerjee et al., 2020 and visual cortex Liu et al., 2020 have revealed that top-down signals from distant cortical regions can modify sensory representations during learning, although the cellular and circuit mechanisms underlying this plasticity remain unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Apical tufts receive top-down signals from numerous cortical and thalamic areas.
source: Apical tufts are anatomically well positioned for learning, receiving top-down signals from numerous cortical and thalamic areas (Zhang and Bruno, 2019; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Cauller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: L5 distal tufts are electrically remote and far from the soma.
source: While L5 distal tufts are electrically remote and far from the soma, they are in close proximity to the highly electrogenic calcium spike initiation zone at the main bifurcation of the apical dendrite, and form a separate biophysical and processing compartment from the proximal dendrites (Amitai et al., 1993; Yuste et al., 1994; Schiller et al., 1997; Larkum et al., 2009; Sandler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biophysical studies.

claim: L5 distal tufts are in close proximity to the highly electrogenic calcium spike initiation zone at the main bifurcation of the apical dendrite.
source: While L5 distal tufts are electrically remote and far from the soma, they are in close proximity to the highly electrogenic calcium spike initiation zone at the main bifurcation of the apical dendrite, and form a separate biophysical and processing compartment from the proximal dendrites (Amitai et al., 1993; Yuste et al., 1994; Schiller et al., 1997; Larkum et al., 2009; Sandler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biophysical studies.

claim: L5 distal tufts form a separate biophysical and processing compartment from the proximal dendrites.
source: While L5 distal tufts are electrically remote and far from the soma, they are in close proximity to the highly electrogenic calcium spike initiation zone at the main bifurcation of the apical dendrite, and form a separate biophysical and processing compartment from the proximal dendrites (Amitai et al., 1993; Yuste et al., 1994; Schiller et al., 1997; Larkum et al., 2009; Sandler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biophysical studies.

claim: Top-down signals arriving at the tuft can trigger tuft-wide dendritic calcium spikes in L5 neurons.
source: Top-down signals arriving at the tuft can trigger tuft-wide dendritic calcium spikes in L5 neurons (Manita et al., 2015), which can modulate synaptic plasticity across the entire dendritic tree Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018 and potently drive somatic burst firing (Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum and Zhu, 2002; Larkum et al., 2004; Schwindt and Crill, 1999; Larkum et al., 2001; Manita et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Tuft-wide dendritic calcium spikes can modulate synaptic plasticity across the entire dendritic tree.
source: Top-down signals arriving at the tuft can trigger tuft-wide dendritic calcium spikes in L5 neurons (Manita et al., 2015), which can modulate synaptic plasticity across the entire dendritic tree Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018 and potently drive somatic burst firing (Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum and Zhu, 2002; Larkum et al., 2004; Schwindt and Crill, 1999; Larkum et al., 2001; Manita et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Tuft-wide dendritic calcium spikes potently drive somatic burst firing.
source: Top-down signals arriving at the tuft can trigger tuft-wide dendritic calcium spikes in L5 neurons (Manita et al., 2015), which can modulate synaptic plasticity across the entire dendritic tree Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018 and potently drive somatic burst firing (Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum and Zhu, 2002; Larkum et al., 2004; Schwindt and Crill, 1999; Larkum et al., 2001; Manita et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: L5 apical dendrite activity is highly correlated with somatic activity.
source: Consistent with this observation, L5 apical dendrite activity is highly correlated with somatic activity (Francioni et al., 2019; Beaulieu-Laroche et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: L5 apical dendritic calcium spikes can play an important role in modulating cortical output by strongly influencing somatic activity.
source: Therefore, by strongly influencing somatic activity, L5 apical dendritic calcium spikes can play an important role in modulating cortical output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited relationship between apical dendrite and somatic activity.

claim: Several neuromodulators can augment the excitability of the apical tuft and increase the likelihood of eliciting calcium spikes.
source: Several neuromodulators can augment the excitability of the apical tuft and increase the likelihood of eliciting calcium spikes (Labarrera et al., 2018; Brombas et al., 2014), which could be a substrate for control of plasticity by behavioral state.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Neuromodulator effects on apical tuft excitability could be a substrate for control of plasticity by behavioral state.
source: Several neuromodulators can augment the excitability of the apical tuft and increase the likelihood of eliciting calcium spikes (Labarrera et al., 2018; Brombas et al., 2014), which could be a substrate for control of plasticity by behavioral state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited findings.

claim: During behavioral training with positive reinforcements, apical tufts in sensory cortex acquire associations that extend beyond their normal sensory modality.
source: Consistent with these ideas, we recently demonstrated that during behavioral training with positive reinforcements, apical tufts in sensory cortex acquire associations that extend beyond their normal sensory modality (Lacefield et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: In mouse models of dementia and Alzheimer's disease, tuft dendrites exhibit degeneration which may contribute to cognitive and memory deficits.
source: In mouse models of dementia and Alzheimer's disease (Luebke et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2004), tuft dendrites exhibit degeneration which may contribute to the cognitive and memory deficits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on disease models, with a speculative interpretation about the functional consequences.

claim: L5 pyramidal neurons are the major source of output from cortex, targeting numerous subcortical structures that affect behavior.
source: L5 pyramidal neurons are the major source of output from cortex, targeting numerous subcortical structures that affect behavior.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The activity of apical dendrites is known to correlate with stimulus intensity.
source: The activity of apical dendrites is known to correlate with stimulus intensity, and manipulating L5 apical dendrites and their inputs impacts performance of sensory tasks (Manita et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Manipulating L5 apical dendrites and their inputs impacts performance of sensory tasks.
source: The activity of apical dendrites is known to correlate with stimulus intensity, and manipulating L5 apical dendrites and their inputs impacts performance of sensory tasks (Manita et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2020; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Apical dendritic calcium spikes of pyramidal cells could be a crucial cellular mechanism in learning-related plasticity and behavioral modification.
source: Apical dendritic calcium spikes of pyramidal cells could be a crucial cellular mechanism in learning-related plasticity and behavioral modification (Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018; Bittner et al., 2017; Doron et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Sensory representations of apical tufts, as well as possible changes across learning, have received little attention.
source: However, sensory representations of apical tufts, as well as possible changes across learning, have received little attention.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: Rodents are known to sense wind direction using their whiskers.
source: In addition to discriminating tactile objects, rodents are known to sense wind direction using their whiskers (Yu et al., 2016a; Yu et al., 2016b) and can be trained to discriminate different directions of whisker deflections (Nakamura et al., 2009; Bernhard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Rodents can be trained to discriminate different directions of whisker deflections.
source: In addition to discriminating tactile objects, rodents are known to sense wind direction using their whiskers (Yu et al., 2016a; Yu et al., 2016b) and can be trained to discriminate different directions of whisker deflections (Nakamura et al., 2009; Bernhard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Brief (100 ms) air puffs were directed at the whiskers in either rostrocaudal (backward) or ventrodorsal (upward) directions.
source: With this in mind, we directed brief (100 ms) air puffs at the whiskers in either of two directions: rostrocaudal (backward) or ventrodorsal (upward).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulus parameters.

claim: One direction was paired with a water reward delivered 500 ms after the air puff and constituted a conditioned stimulus (CS+).
source: One of the directions was paired with a water reward delivered 500 ms after the air puff and thus constituted a conditioned stimulus (CS+).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: No reward was given for the other direction (CS-).
source: No reward was given for the other direction (CS-).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Stimuli elicited a brief passive whisker deflection followed by active whisking over the subsequent ~1.5 s.
source: Stimuli elicited a brief passive whisker deflection followed by active whisking over the subsequent ~1.5 s (analyzed below, Figure 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: On the first session, mice exhibited few anticipatory licks to either stimulus.
source: Typically, on the first session, mice exhibited few anticipatory licks to either stimulus (Figure 1c, top, grey shading).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: By session 2 or 3, mice had learned an association between whisker deflection and reward, but could not discriminate the CS+ and CS-.
source: By session 2 or 3, mice had learned an association between whisker deflection and reward, but could not discriminate the CS+ and CS- (middle).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Within a week (by sessions 7–9), every mouse learned to reliably lick to the CS+ while withholding licks to the CS-.
source: Within a week (by sessions 7–9), every mouse we tested learned to reliably lick to the CS+ while withholding licks to the CS-, performing substantially above chance after a single week of training (Figure 1c, bottom; Figure 1e and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data shown in Figures 1c, 1e, and 1f.

claim: Mice performed substantially above chance after a single week of training.
source: Within a week (by sessions 7–9), every mouse we tested learned to reliably lick to the CS+ while withholding licks to the CS-, performing substantially above chance after a single week of training (Figure 1c, bottom; Figure 1e and f).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data shown in Figures 1e and 1f.

claim: Mice rapidly learned to discriminate the direction of whisker stimuli in the behavioral task.
source: Thus, mice rapidly learned to discriminate the direction of whisker stimuli in our behavioral task.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral data.

claim: Apical tufts were imaged across conditioning days as well as on an unrewarded pre-conditioning day and an unrewarded post-conditioning day.
source: To investigate the effects of reinforcement learning on apical tuft activity, we imaged apical tufts (433x433 μm field of view) across conditioning days as well as on an unrewarded pre-conditioning day to measure naïve stimulus responses and an unrewarded post-conditioning day to detect any long-lasting changes in responses (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The gene for Cre-dependent GCaMP6f was virally delivered in the barrel cortex of Rbp4-Cre mice.
source: We virally delivered the gene for Cre-dependent GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) in the barrel cortex of Rbp4-Cre mice, which labels a heterogeneous population of pyramidal neurons comprising approximately 50% of layer 5 (Lacefield et al., 2019; Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012; Glickfeld et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Rbp4-Cre mice label a heterogeneous population of pyramidal neurons comprising approximately 50% of layer 5.
source: We virally delivered the gene for Cre-dependent GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) in the barrel cortex of Rbp4-Cre mice, which labels a heterogeneous population of pyramidal neurons comprising approximately 50% of layer 5 (Lacefield et al., 2019; Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012; Glickfeld et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing this mouse line.

claim: By targeting injections to layer 5B, thick-tufted pyramidal neurons were predominantly labeled.
source: By targeting our injections to layer 5B, we predominantly labeled thick-tufted pyramidal neurons (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the targeting strategy used in the experiments.

claim: Intrinsic signal imaging was used to map the location of the C2, D2, and gamma whisker barrel columns.
source: Using intrinsic signal imaging, we mapped the location of the C2, D2, and gamma whisker barrel columns and identified an overlapping region in layer 1 with sufficient GCaMP6f expression (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes the experimental method shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Dendritic activity was longitudinally recorded from the same field-of-view across all sessions.
source: Dendritic activity was longitudinally recorded from the same field-of-view (horizontal location and depth) in layer 1 across all sessions (Video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Individual segmented tufts were substantial in their spatial extent (>100 µm), reflecting tuft-wide voltage-gated calcium spikes rather than branch-specific NMDA receptor-mediated spikes.
source: Individual segmented tufts were substantial in their spatial extent (>100 µm), reflecting tuft-wide voltage-gated calcium spikes rather than branch-specific N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor-mediated spikes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data based on the spatial extent of the signals.

claim: Successful calcium events across tufts averaged 28% ΔF/F.
source: Successful calcium events across tufts averaged 28% ΔF/F, consistent with previous studies of layer 5 apical dendrites (Manita et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the imaging data, compared to previous studies.

claim: During intermediate but not early learning, the average population response to the CS+ exhibited a two-peak structure.
source: Interestingly, during intermediate but not early learning, the average population response to the CS+ exhibited a two-peak structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, session 4) similar to tuft reward-related signals we observed previously in barrel cortex (Lacefield et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: By the last-rewarded and post sessions, the second CS+ peak was no longer visible.
source: By the last-rewarded and post sessions, the second CS+ peak was no longer visible, which could be an endpoint of mice learning that the conditioned stimulus predicts the upcoming reward.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Average responses of tufts to the CS+ and CS- were similar during the pre-conditioning session.
source: Average responses of tufts to the CS+ and CS- were similar during the pre-conditioning session (Figure 2d; p=0.20, signed rank test, n=440 pre tufts and 418 post tufts), indicating that there was no inherent bias in the population toward a particular stimulus in naïve animals.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: There was no inherent bias in the population toward a particular stimulus in naïve animals.
source: Average responses of tufts to the CS+ and CS- were similar during the pre-conditioning session (Figure 2d; p=0.20, signed rank test, n=440 pre tufts and 418 post tufts), indicating that there was no inherent bias in the population toward a particular stimulus in naïve animals.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis of the imaging data.

claim: After learning, responses to the CS+ and CS- were similar on the last- and post-conditioning sessions.
source: Surprisingly, even after learning, responses to the CS+ and CS- were similar on the last- and post-conditioning sessions (p=0.62, 0.64, respectively, signed rank test, Figure 2d and e), revealing that no bias develops for the CS+ among dendritic tufts.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figures 2d and 2e.

claim: No bias develops for the CS+ among dendritic tufts after learning.
source: Surprisingly, even after learning, responses to the CS+ and CS- were similar on the last- and post-conditioning sessions (p=0.62, 0.64, respectively, signed rank test, Figure 2d and e), revealing that no bias develops for the CS+ among dendritic tufts.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analysis of the imaging data.

claim: Only a minority of tufts exhibited statistically significant average responses to air puff stimuli (CS+ responsive: 26 ± 8%; CS- responsive: 25 ± 8%).
source: Only a minority of tufts exhibited statistically significant (see Methods) average responses to air puff stimuli (CS+ responsive: 26 ± 8%; CS- responsive: 25 ± 8%; mean ± SD across all sessions).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the imaging data.

claim: When excluding responses that were not statistically significant, there was no difference between the average response amplitudes to the CS+ and CS- on the pre, last-rewarded, and post sessions.
source: When we excluded responses that were not statistically significant, we again found no difference between the average response amplitudes to the CS+ and CS- on the pre, last-rewarded, and post sessions (p=0.65, 0.31, and 0.69, respectively, rank sum test; data not shown).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data.

claim: The probability of transients in response to CS+ versus CS- did not differ during pre-conditioning or post-conditioning sessions.
source: Similarly, the probability of transients in response to CS+ versus CS- (see Methods) did not differ during pre-conditioning or post-conditioning sessions (p=0.66 and p=0.44, respectively, data not shown).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data.

claim: Reinforcement learning in this paradigm does not bias tuft representations toward the rewarded stimulus.
source: Therefore, reinforcement learning in our paradigm does not bias tuft representations toward the rewarded stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analyses of the imaging data.

claim: Conditioning session number was a poor predictor of both CS+ and CS- amplitudes.
source: Linear regression analysis revealed that conditioning session number was a poor predictor of both CS+ and CS- amplitudes (All tufts R2, CS+: 0.0064, CS-: 0.0035, Figure 2e; Significantly responding tufts R2, CS+: 0.014, CS-: 0.014, data not shown).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from regression analysis of the imaging data.

claim: There was a small but significant decrease in amplitude from pre to last for CS+ and CS-.
source: We did find a small but significant decrease in amplitude from pre to last for CS+ (p<0.01) and CS- (p<10–7), but this was not permanent: amplitudes did not significantly differ between the pre and post sessions (Figure 2d; p=0.53, 0.33, CS+ and CS- respectively, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Amplitudes did not significantly differ between the pre and post sessions.
source: We did find a small but significant decrease in amplitude from pre to last for CS+ (p<0.01) and CS- (p<10–7), but this was not permanent: amplitudes did not significantly differ between the pre and post sessions (Figure 2d; p=0.53, 0.33, CS+ and CS- respectively, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Reinforcement learning does not robustly bias the magnitudes of tuft calcium responses to either stimulus at the population level.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that reinforcement learning does not robustly bias the magnitudes of tuft calcium responses to either stimulus at the population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analyses of the imaging data.

claim: Barrel cortex neurons are tuned to the angle of whisker deflection.
source: Barrel cortex neurons are tuned to the angle of whisker deflection (Bruno et al., 2003; Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Ramirez et al., 2014), indicating that the sets of synaptic connections activated by the CS+ and CS- may be overlapping but should not be identical.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The sets of synaptic connections activated by the CS+ and CS- may be overlapping but should not be identical.
source: Barrel cortex neurons are tuned to the angle of whisker deflection (Bruno et al., 2003; Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Ramirez et al., 2014), indicating that the sets of synaptic connections activated by the CS+ and CS- may be overlapping but should not be identical.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies about angular tuning.

claim: Responses to the CS+ and CS- can change independently of each other.
source: Therefore, the possibility exists that responses to the CS+ and CS- can change independently of each other.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the previous statement about overlapping but non-identical synaptic connections.

claim: There was no significant bias in response amplitude toward CS+ or CS- during any of the three sessions (pre, last-rewarded, post).
source: In agreement with our previous analysis, we found no significant bias in response amplitude toward CS+ or CS- during any of the three sessions (Figure 3a; Pre: p=0.20; last-rewarded: p=0.43; Post: p=0.64, sign-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Under naive conditions during the pre session, most tufts that responded to air puff stimuli did not strongly prefer the CS+ or CS-.
source: Under naive conditions during the pre session, most tufts that responded to air puff stimuli did not strongly prefer the CS+ or CS- (Figure 3a, left).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: On the last-rewarded session and the unrewarded post-conditioning session, many tufts exhibited more selective responses to one stimulus or the other.
source: Surprisingly, on the last-rewarded session and the unrewarded post-conditioning session, we observed a prominent shift in the response distribution, where many tufts exhibited more selective responses to one stimulus or the other (Figure 3a, middle and right).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Repeated exposure mice exhibited a stable distribution of response selectivity over time.
source: Repeated exposure mice exhibited a stable distribution of response selectivity over time (Figure 3b; a separate cohort of 7 mice; 317, 313, and 321 tufts on Day 1, Day 8, and Day 9, respectively).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Reinforcement learning, and not simply repeated stimulus exposure, drives apical tufts to become more selective for either the CS+ or CS-.
source: These results suggest that reinforcement learning, and not simply repeated stimulus exposure, drives apical tufts to become more selective for either the CS+ or CS-.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the conditioned and repeated exposure groups.

claim: Initially in both the conditioned and repeated exposure mice, the SI distribution was centered around zero, indicating that most tufts in naïve animals did not strongly prefer either stimulus.
source: Initially in both the conditioned and repeated exposure mice, the SI distribution was centered around zero, indicating that most tufts in naïve animals did not strongly prefer either stimulus (Figure 3c and d, left panels).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: The mean SI remained close to zero for each of the three sessions.
source: Consistent with our other analyses (Figure 2d), the mean SI remained close to zero for each of the three sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d; −0.049,–0.001, and 0.003 for pre-conditioning, last rewarded, and post-conditioning days, respectively; one-way ANOVA p=0.37), confirming that learning produced no overall bias toward one particular stimulus among the population.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Learning produced no overall bias toward one particular stimulus among the population.
source: Consistent with our other analyses (Figure 2d), the mean SI remained close to zero for each of the three sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d; −0.049,–0.001, and 0.003 for pre-conditioning, last rewarded, and post-conditioning days, respectively; one-way ANOVA p=0.37), confirming that learning produced no overall bias toward one particular stimulus among the population.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analysis.

claim: During learning, the SI distribution of conditioned but not repeated exposure mice shifted markedly, whereby a much greater proportion of neurons were highly selective for either the CS+ or CS-.
source: During learning, the SI distribution of conditioned but not repeated exposure mice shifted markedly, whereby a much greater proportion of neurons were highly selective for either the CS+ or CS- (Figure 3c and d, middle and right panels, |SI| pre versus last-rewarded: p<10–6, |SI| pre versus post: p<10–5; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: Learning significantly increased tuft selectivity in individual conditioned mice, but not repeated exposure mice.
source: Learning significantly increased tuft selectivity in individual conditioned mice, but not repeated exposure mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The degree of enhancement in tuft selectivity was closely correlated with conditioned animals' ability to discriminate stimuli across sessions.
source: The degree of enhancement in tuft selectivity was closely correlated with conditioned animals' ability to discriminate stimuli across sessions (Figure 3e; Pearson's r=0.60, p<10–5).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Neural discriminability was correlated with behavioral performance.
source: Similar to selectivity magnitude, we found that neural discriminability was correlated with behavioral performance (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3f.

claim: In conditioned animals, neural discriminability of CS+ and CS- responses of tufts increased significantly across learning.
source: In conditioned animals, neural discriminability of CS+ and CS- responses of tufts increased significantly across learning (Figure 3g, blue; first-rewarded versus last-rewarded: p<10–3, pre versus post: p<10–4; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Neural discriminability of tuft responses in the repeated exposure mice decreased slightly with progressive exposure to the stimuli.
source: By contrast, neural discriminability of tuft responses in the repeated exposure mice decreased slightly with progressive exposure to the stimuli (Figure 3g, gray; Day 1 versus Final: p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Decoder performance increased significantly when comparing Pre and First sessions to Post and Last sessions in conditioned mice.
source: We found that decoder performance increased significantly when comparing Pre and First sessions to Post and Last sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a; sign-rank test, p=0.002), whereas decoder performance did not improve over time in the repeated exposure mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b; sign-rank test, p=0.22).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the decoder analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Decoder performance did not improve over time in the repeated exposure mice.
source: We found that decoder performance increased significantly when comparing Pre and First sessions to Post and Last sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a; sign-rank test, p=0.002), whereas decoder performance did not improve over time in the repeated exposure mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b; sign-rank test, p=0.22).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the decoder analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Enhanced stimulus representations can emerge in apical tufts, but require reinforcement.
source: Taken together, these results show that enhanced stimulus representations can emerge in apical tufts, but require reinforcement.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comparison of conditioned and repeated exposure groups.

claim: Two-photon microscopy acquires images with high resolution and speed, but the imaging field is restricted to a single focal plane.
source: While two-photon microscopy acquires images with high resolution and speed, the imaging field is restricted to a single focal plane.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of two-photon microscopy.

claim: Two-photon microscopy can only measure calcium signals from a thin cross-section of the three-dimensionally complex apical structures.
source: This method can only measure calcium signals from a thin cross-section of the three-dimensionally complex apical structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of two-photon microscopy.

claim: Many of the spatial components extracted from two-photon data were comprised of dendritic branches that cross the imaging plane at different locations.
source: Indeed, many of the spatial components extracted from our two-photon data were comprised of dendritic branches that cross the imaging plane at different locations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), which makes it difficult to determine whether the segmentation software accurately extracted signals from one tuft or erroneously merged multiple tufts.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A single apical tuft could be falsely classified as two different tufts.
source: For the same reasons, a single apical tuft could be falsely classified as two different tufts.
evidence: This is a potential technical concern about segmentation.

claim: SCAPE microscopy allowed monitoring of calcium across entire apical tufts.
source: To confirm that our interpretation was not due to segmentation errors, we repeated the conditioning experiment using a high-speed volumetric imaging approach called SCAPE (Bouchard et al., 2015; Hillman et al., 2018), which allowed us to monitor calcium across entire apical tufts (Video 2).
evidence: This describes the technical capability of SCAPE microscopy.

claim: Three-dimensional SCAPE datasets encompassed large portions of the apical tree which included branches converging on their bifurcation points in layer 2, enabling unambiguous identification of whole apical trees.
source: These three-dimensional datasets (300×1050 × 234 μm field of view) encompassed large portions of the apical tree which included branches converging on their bifurcation points in layer 2, enabling us to identify whole apical trees unambiguously (Figure 4a and b; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This describes the advantage of SCAPE microscopy shown in Figures 4a, 4b, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Task learning induced significant increases in tuft selectivity as measured by SCAPE microscopy.
source: Comparison of tuft responses to the CS+ and CS- on the pre, last-rewarded, and post sessions (Figure 4d; 241 pre, 215 last-rewarded, 150 post tufts in 2 mice) revealed again that task learning induced significant increases in tuft selectivity (Figure 4e; pre versus last-rewarded: p<10–5, pre versus post: p<10–4, Wilcoxon rank sum test of |SI|).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the SCAPE imaging data shown in Figures 4d and 4e.

claim: The SI magnitudes were similar between tufts imaged using two-photon microscopy and SCAPE.
source: On average, the SI magnitudes were similar between tufts imaged using two-photon microscopy and SCAPE (mean ± s.e.m. |SI| for two-photon versus SCAPE; pre: 0.41±0.01 vs 0.40±0.02; last-rewarded: 0.54±0.02 vs 0.54±0.02; post: 0.51±0.02 vs 0.53±0.03).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the two imaging methods.

claim: The effects observed in the two-photon dataset are not caused by errors in segmentation, but rather reflect changes at the level of individual dendritic tufts.
source: These data demonstrate that the effects in our two-photon dataset are not caused by errors in segmentation, but rather reflect changes at the level of individual dendritic tufts.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the two-photon and SCAPE results.

claim: Reinforcement increases stimulus selectivity at the level of the entire apical tuft.
source: Our results, based on two different imaging approaches, clearly demonstrate that reinforcement increases stimulus selectivity at the level of the entire apical tuft.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined two-photon and SCAPE results.

claim: Approximately 40% of initially unresponsive tufts developed a response to at least one stimulus by the last session in both conditioned and repeated exposure mice.
source: Interestingly, in both the conditioned and repeated exposure mice, approximately 40% of initially unresponsive tufts developed a response to at least one stimulus by the last session, becoming either selective or unselective (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal tracking shown in Figure 5b.

claim: In conditioned animals, the proportion of initially unresponsive tufts that became selective was significantly larger than in repeated exposure mice.
source: However, in conditioned animals, the proportion of initially unresponsive tufts that became selective was significantly larger than in repeated exposure mice (Figure 5b; p=0.04, 2-sample t-test comparing mice).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from longitudinal tracking shown in Figure 5b.

claim: While the proportion of selective and unselective tufts in the initially unresponsive category was similar for conditioned animals, unselective tufts were more common in repeated exposure mice.
source: Furthermore, while the proportion of selective and unselective tufts in this category was similar for conditioned animals, unselective tufts were more common in repeated exposure mice (Figure 5b; p=0.03, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from longitudinal tracking shown in Figure 5b.

claim: While both stimulus exposure and reinforcement can alter tuft tuning, the presence of reward increases the likelihood that initially unresponsive tufts develop selectivity for either the CS+ or CS-.
source: Together, these results indicate that, while both stimulus exposure and reinforcement can alter tuft tuning, the presence of reward increases the likelihood that initially unresponsive tufts develop selectivity for either the CS+ or CS- (summarized in Figure 5e).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the longitudinal tracking analysis summarized in Figure 5e.

claim: The SI distribution of initially unresponsive tufts on the final imaging session was shifted toward the tails in conditioned, but not repeated exposure mice.
source: Supporting our results in Figure 5b, the SI distribution was shifted toward the tails in conditioned, but not repeated exposure mice, indicating that reward enhances selectivity for either the CS+ or CS- in this subset (|SI| conditioned versus repeated exposure: p<10–5, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n=199 and 110 tufts, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the longitudinal tracking shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Among selective tufts, the |SI| distribution in conditioned mice was significantly greater than in repeated exposure mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that even among selective tufts, the |SI| distribution in conditioned mice was significantly greater than in repeated exposure mice (p=0.006, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n=122 and 47 tufts, respectively), indicating that while selective tufts are present after both conditioning and repeated stimulus exposure, the magnitude of selectivity is stronger after conditioning.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the longitudinal tracking shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Tufts in conditioned mice exhibited a greater increase in |SI| across sessions compared to repeated exposure mice.
source: Tufts in conditioned mice exhibited a greater increase in |SI| across sessions compared to repeated exposure mice (p=0.01, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n=48 and 42 tufts, respectively), demonstrating that the magnitude of selectivity in initially responsive tufts increases after reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the longitudinal tracking shown in Figure 5h.

claim: The magnitude of selectivity in initially responsive tufts increases after reinforcement learning.
source: Tufts in conditioned mice exhibited a greater increase in |SI| across sessions compared to repeated exposure mice (p=0.01, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n=48 and 42 tufts, respectively), demonstrating that the magnitude of selectivity in initially responsive tufts increases after reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Tufts that became unresponsive were more likely to be initially highly selective in the conditioned group than in the repeated exposure group.
source: However, tufts that became unresponsive were more likely to be initially highly selective in the conditioned group than in the repeated exposure group (19 tufts with initial |SI|>0.75 / 97 tufts ending as unresponsive in the conditioned group versus 3/81 in the repeated exposure group; p=0.0013, Z approximation to binomial).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the longitudinal tracking.

claim: Learning can involve a loss of responsivity in a small subset of well-tuned tufts.
source: Therefore, learning can involve a loss of responsivity in a small subset of well-tuned tufts.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the longitudinal tracking analysis.

claim: Reinforcement learning biases initially unresponsive tufts toward becoming selective and enhances the selectivity of tufts that are initially responsive.
source: In summary, our longitudinal analyses revealed that reinforcement learning biases initially unresponsive tufts toward becoming selective and enhances the selectivity of tufts that are initially responsive.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the longitudinal tracking analyses.

claim: Whisking is correlated with layer 5 somatic action potentials.
source: For instance, movements like whisking are correlated with layer 5 somatic action potentials (Derdikman et al., 2006; de Kock and Sakmann, 2009; Rodgers et al., 2021) and might have impacted calcium activity in the apical tuft.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The magnitudes of whisker movements following both stimuli were stable across sessions.
source: Although conditioning alters licking behavior (Figure 1c and e), the magnitudes of whisker movements following both stimuli were stable across sessions (Figure 6b; CS+: p=0.44; CS-: p=0.45; linear regression).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the whisking analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The whisking amplitude became slightly more reliable (decreased SD) across sessions.
source: We also computed the standard deviation (SD) of stimulus-evoked whisker amplitude across trials for all sessions (Figure 6c). While the whisking amplitude became slightly more reliable (decreased SD) across sessions (p<10–4), the change in reliability across sessions was similar for CS+ and CS- (p=0.53).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the whisking analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The change in whisking reliability across sessions was similar for CS+ and CS-.
source: We also computed the standard deviation (SD) of stimulus-evoked whisker amplitude across trials for all sessions (Figure 6c). While the whisking amplitude became slightly more reliable (decreased SD) across sessions (p<10–4), the change in reliability across sessions was similar for CS+ and CS- (p=0.53).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the whisking analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Whisking is similar on both trial types throughout learning.
source: Therefore, whisking is similar on both trial types throughout learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the whisking analysis.

claim: Whisking amplitude was similar between spontaneous ITI whisking bouts and evoked whisking responses to stimuli.
source: Whisking amplitude was similar between spontaneous ITI whisking bouts and evoked whisking responses to stimuli (n=115 and 617 events, respectively; p=0.53, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the whisking analysis.

claim: ITI whisking bouts were not associated with a robust calcium response.
source: In contrast to air puff stimuli, ITI whisking bouts were not associated with a robust calcium response (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Air puff stimuli more reliably predicted calcium influx than whisking amplitude for virtually all tufts.
source: Air puff stimuli more reliably predicted calcium influx than whisking amplitude for each of virtually all tufts (p<10–12, sign rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the regression analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: There was no relationship between the whisking response and the median SI magnitude on a given session.
source: Furthermore, we found no relationship between the whisking response and the median SI magnitude on a given session (Figure 6f, whisking to CS+ p = 0.22, CS- p=0.78).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Changes in whisker movement cannot account for the changes in selectivity during learning.
source: Therefore, changes in whisker movement cannot account for the changes in selectivity during learning that we observed.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the whisking analyses.

claim: Behaviorally modulated tufts accounted for only ~10% of the total tuft population in both early and late learning.
source: Behaviorally modulated tufts accounted for only ~10% of the total tuft population in both early and late learning (50/395 in early; 35/406 in late learning).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the behavioral modulation analysis.

claim: Selectivity increased significantly from early to late learning when behaviorally modulated tufts were excluded.
source: We found that selectivity increased significantly from early to late learning (Figure 7b and c; median |SI| of 345 tufts early versus 371 tufts late learning: 0.38 vs 0.47, p=0.02, Wilcoxon rank sum test), similar to our previous analysis of the entire population.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis shown in Figures 7b and 7c.

claim: Licking was a relatively poor predictor of tuft calcium influx.
source: Licking, like whisking, was a relatively poor predictor of tuft calcium influx (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Median coefficients for licking and whisking were on average 3.3 times smaller than median stimulus coefficients for the first rewarded, last rewarded, and post sessions.
source: Median coefficients for licking and whisking were on average 3.3 times smaller than median stimulus coefficients for the first rewarded, last rewarded, and post sessions (all p<10–6, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the multivariate regression analysis.

claim: CS+ and CS- coefficients were enhanced by learning but not repeated exposure after factoring out possible effects of movements.
source: Even after we factored out possible effects of movements, CS+ and CS- coefficients were enhanced by learning but not repeated exposure (Figure 7—figure supplement 1c and d), consistent with our other analyses.
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariate regression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enhanced selectivity during learning cannot be explained by non-sensory signals related to the animals' behavior.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that enhanced selectivity during learning cannot be explained by non-sensory signals related to the animals' behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral modulation and regression analyses.

claim: Performance in each of the five mice decreased after whisker trimming, indicating that each used some whisker information.
source: Performance in each of the five mice decreased after whisker trimming, indicating that each used some whisker information.
evidence: This is a finding from the whisker trimming experiment.

claim: Three mice performed the task exclusively with their whiskers, falling to chance levels after the whisker trim.
source: Three mice performed the task exclusively with their whiskers, falling to chance levels after the whisker trim ('whiskers only').
evidence: This is a finding from the whisker trimming experiment.

claim: Two mice still performed the task above chance after the whisker trim, indicating that they were not exclusively using their whiskers and exploited information from multiple sensory streams.
source: Two other mice still performed the task above chance after the whisker trim, indicating that they were not exclusively using their whiskers and exploited information from multiple sensory streams ('whiskers + other senses').
evidence: This is a finding from the whisker trimming experiment.

claim: Both the 'whiskers only' and 'whiskers + other senses' groups exhibited enhanced tuft selectivity in the last-rewarded session relative to pre-conditioning.
source: Both the 'whiskers only' and 'whiskers + other senses' groups exhibited enhanced tuft selectivity in the last-rewarded session relative to pre-conditioning.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the two groups shown in Figures 8a and 8b.

claim: The enhancement in tuft selectivity was more pronounced in the 'whiskers only' mice.
source: This effect was more pronounced in the 'whiskers only' mice (Figure 8a and b, left and middle; whiskers only: median |SI| of 180 pre tufts versus 169 last-rewarded tufts: 0.36 vs 0.59, p<10–3; 'whiskers + other senses': median |SI| of 144 pre tufts versus 155 last-rewarded tufts: 0.39 vs 0.50, p=0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figures 8a and 8b.

claim: Enhanced selectivity persisted during the post-conditioning session for the 'whiskers only' group but not the 'whiskers + other senses' group.
source: Surprisingly, enhanced selectivity persisted during the post-conditioning session for the 'whiskers only' group but not the 'whiskers + other senses' group (Figure 8a and b right panels; whiskers only: median |SI| of pre versus 167 tufts post: 0.36 vs 0.58; p<10–3; whiskers + other senses: median |SI| of 155 pre versus post tufts: 0.39 vs 0.42; p=0.45).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figures 8a and 8b.

claim: Tuft selectivity in barrel cortex is enhanced regardless of behavioral strategy, but outlasts conditioning only when mice rely solely on their whiskers to perform the task.
source: Therefore, tuft selectivity in barrel cortex is enhanced regardless of behavioral strategy, but outlasts conditioning only when mice rely solely on their whiskers to perform the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the two behavioral strategy groups.

claim: By the second half of the post-conditioning session, the probability of a lick occurring during the CS+ extinguished, approaching zero.
source: By the second half of the session, the probability of a lick occurring during the CS+ extinguished, approaching zero (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Selectivity of tufts remained stable throughout the post-conditioning session in mice that exclusively used their whiskers.
source: We compared the selectivity of tufts during the first and second halves of the post-conditioning sessions of mice that exclusively used their whiskers and found no difference in the two distributions (Figure 8d, p=0.94, Wilcoxon rank sum test of |SI|), demonstrating that selectivity of the population remained stable throughout the session.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the imaging data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Enhanced stimulus selectivity of apical tuft dendrites after reinforcement learning is long lasting, persisting even after mice cease performing the task and expecting reward.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that enhanced stimulus selectivity of apical tuft dendrites after reinforcement learning is long lasting, persisting even after mice cease performing the task and expecting reward.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the post-conditioning analyses.

claim: This study is the first to investigate how learning a discrimination task alters apical tuft activity.
source: Our study is the first to investigate how learning a discrimination task alters apical tuft activity.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: L5 apical tufts acquire enhanced representations of multiple stimuli during learning.
source: Using both novel volumetric whole-tuft imaging and conventional planar microscopy, we discovered that L5 apical tufts acquire enhanced representations of multiple stimuli during learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Learning enhanced selectivity for both stimuli, suggesting that tufts are aligning themselves to the behaviorally relevant stimulus dimensions.
source: Rather than simply retuning tufts toward the rewarded stimulus, learning enhanced selectivity for both stimuli, suggesting that tufts are aligning themselves to the behaviorally relevant stimulus dimensions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the main finding.

claim: The enhancement of selectivity for both stimuli is particularly striking given that the two stimuli are in orthogonal not opposing directions.
source: This effect is particularly striking given that, by design, the two stimuli are in orthogonal not opposing directions.
evidence: This is a comment on the significance of the finding in relation to the experimental design.

claim: Enhanced sensory representations persist even after mice cease performing the task.
source: These enhanced sensory representations persist even after mice cease performing the task.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.

claim: Representations are slightly degraded by mere repeated exposure to stimuli outside of a task.
source: In contrast, representations are slightly degraded by mere repeated exposure to stimuli outside of a task.
evidence: This is a summary of the control group findings.

claim: Movement in and of itself has little direct impact on tuft spikes.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Lacefield et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2012), we found that movement in and of itself has little direct impact on tuft spikes, indicating that increased selectivity of apicals reflects alterations in sensory coding as animals learn.
evidence: This is a finding from the movement analysis, consistent with previous studies.

claim: Increased selectivity of apicals reflects alterations in sensory coding as animals learn.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Lacefield et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2012), we found that movement in and of itself has little direct impact on tuft spikes, indicating that increased selectivity of apicals reflects alterations in sensory coding as animals learn.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the movement analysis findings.

claim: Sensitization of tufts to behaviorally relevant sensory dimensions may be a general feature of all sensory cortical areas.
source: This sensitization of tufts to behaviorally relevant sensory dimensions may be a general feature of all sensory cortical areas.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization of the findings.

claim: Tuft spikes enhance plasticity of synaptic inputs that occur over behavioral (seconds-long) timescales.
source: Tuft spikes enhance plasticity of synaptic inputs that occur over behavioral (seconds-long) timescales (Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018; Bittner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: New behaviorally relevant tuft representations may prime subsequent plasticity of synapses across the entire pyramidal neuron.
source: These new behaviorally relevant tuft representations may therefore prime subsequent plasticity of synapses across the entire pyramidal neuron.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the cited literature.

claim: Tuft events potently modulate somatic burst firing and enhance how somata respond to their basal inputs.
source: Additionally, tuft events potently modulate somatic burst firing and enhance how somata respond to their basal inputs (Larkum et al., 2009; Larkum, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: As learning and plasticity increase apical selectivity for a behaviorally relevant axis, tuft events will unavoidably amplify somatic burst output along the same axis.
source: As learning and plasticity increase apical selectivity for a behaviorally relevant axis, tuft events will unavoidably amplify somatic burst output along the same axis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited relationship between tuft events and somatic output.

claim: Enhanced tuft selectivity could enable action potential output of L5 cells in primary sensory cortex to directly drive behavioral responses via projections to movement related areas.
source: This could enable action potential output of L5 cells in primary sensory cortex to directly drive behavioral responses via projections to movement related areas, such as the corticostriatal, corticopontine, and corticotrigeminal pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional consequences of the findings.

claim: Tuft spikes have the potential to modify somatic output, both in the present and in the future.
source: Thus, tuft spikes have the potential to modify somatic output, both in the present and in the future.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the potential functional impact of tuft spikes.

claim: Enhancing the representation of relevant stimulus dimensions rather than a singularly important stimulus has multiple benefits for behavior.
source: Enhancing the representation of relevant stimulus dimensions rather than a singularly important stimulus, such as a rewarded event, has multiple benefits for behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: In the task, both the CS+ and CS- are predictive of whether or not a reward will occur in the future.
source: In our paradigm, both the CS+ and CS- are predictive of whether or not a reward will occur in the future.
evidence: This is a statement about the task design.

claim: Explicitly encoding both stimuli could allow sensory cortical areas to directly elicit actions.
source: Explicitly encoding both stimuli could allow sensory cortical areas to directly elicit actions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance.

claim: CS+ preferring tufts in barrel cortex may trigger anticipatory licking while CS- preferring tufts could suppress licking.
source: In the context of this task, CS+ preferring tufts in barrel cortex may trigger anticipatory licking while CS- preferring tufts could suppress licking.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how the neural representations might drive behavior.

claim: L5 cells in sensory cortex via their output to striatum, pons, brain stem, and spinal cord would be able to directly and rapidly drive action without further cortical processing.
source: L5 cells in sensory cortex via their output to striatum, pons, brain stem, and spinal cord would thereby be able to directly and rapidly drive action without further cortical processing, such as by frontal areas including motor cortex (Takahashi et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Rapid sensory-motor transformations by primary sensory areas may be critical for natural time-constrained behavior.
source: Such rapid sensory-motor transformations by primary sensory areas may be critical for natural time-constrained behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance.

claim: Learning produced a representation in which the degree of selectivity for the two stimuli was continuous and uniformly distributed.
source: Furthermore, learning produced a representation in which the degree of selectivity for the two stimuli was continuous and uniformly distributed.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.

claim: Exclusively CS+ or CS- selective apicals never dominated the population.
source: Exclusively CS+ or CS- selective apicals never dominated the population.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.

claim: Continuous degrees of selectivity across the population may allow the system to be more robust to the variability caused by active movements that alter sensory input.
source: Continuous degrees of selectivity across the population, rather than discrete representations, may allow the system to be more robust to the variability caused by active movements that alter sensory input.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the continuous distribution.

claim: A continuous distribution may facilitate future adjustments of neural representations as subjects continue to learn a task or encounter new tasks.
source: A continuous distribution may also facilitate future adjustments of neural representations as subjects continue to learn a task or encounter new tasks.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the continuous distribution.

claim: The uniformity observed may reflect that neurons are high-dimensional, being sensitive to mixtures of variables, only one of which might be altered by learning.
source: The uniformity we observed may reflect that neurons are high-dimensional, being sensitive to mixtures of variables (Rodgers et al., 2021; Rigotti et al., 2013; Stringer et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2020), only one of which might be altered here by learning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to studies on high-dimensional neural representations.

claim: The uniform distribution of selectivity corresponds to a full range of pessimism to optimism concerning stimulus predictions of upcoming rewards.
source: The uniform distribution of selectivity corresponds to a full range of pessimism to optimism concerning stimulus predictions of upcoming rewards.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the uniform distribution might represent.

claim: Behavioral performance benefits from reinforcement learning that incorporates the distribution of reward probabilities rather than just the average expected reward value.
source: Recent work shows that behavioral performance benefits from reinforcement learning that incorporates the distribution of reward probabilities rather than just the average expected reward value (Dabney et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: L5 corticostriatal synapses could theoretically afford a plastic substrate for acquiring the necessary distribution of reward probabilities.
source: L5 corticostriatal synapses could theoretically afford a plastic substrate for acquiring the necessary distribution of reward probabilities.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the findings to the cited work on distributional reinforcement learning.

claim: Past studies in which mice were trained to associate one or more stimuli with a reward typically show that cortical representations are stronger for the rewarded stimulus.
source: Surprisingly, past studies in which mice were trained to associate one or more stimuli with a reward typically show that cortical representations are stronger for the rewarded stimulus (Poort et al., 2015; Henschke et al., 2020; Goltstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The overall tuft calcium response to the CS+ and CS- at the population level did not change significantly after animals learned the task.
source: In contrast to these studies of layer 2/3 somatic activity, our experiments revealed that the overall tuft calcium response to the CS+ and CS- at the population level did not change significantly after animals learned the task (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding shown in Figure 2.

claim: Representations for both stimuli were enhanced by individual tufts developing selectivity for either the CS+ or the CS-.
source: Instead, representations for both stimuli were enhanced by individual tufts developing selectivity for either the CS+ or the CS- (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding shown in Figure 3.

claim: Enhanced selectivity for both rewarded and unrewarded stimuli could be a phenomenon that is unique to the apical dendritic tufts.
source: First, enhanced selectivity for both rewarded and unrewarded stimuli could be a phenomenon that is unique to the apical dendritic tufts.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the divergence from previous studies.

claim: The apical tufts of pyramidal cells in S1 receive long-range top-down input from several sources, including motor cortex, secondary somatosensory cortex, and secondary thalamus.
source: In addition to local inputs, the apical tufts of pyramidal cells in S1 receive long-range top-down input from several sources, including motor cortex (Xu et al., 2012; Petreanu et al., 2012), secondary somatosensory cortex (Cauller et al., 1998), and secondary thalamus (Zhang and Bruno, 2019; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Wimmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Frontal areas have enhanced representations of the CS+ and CS- after learning.
source: Frontal areas, such as prefrontal cortex, indeed have enhanced representations of the CS+ and CS- after learning (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Input to the somata is dominated by the local cortical area and primary thalamus.
source: In contrast, input to the somata is dominated by the local cortical area and primary thalamus (Feldmeyer, 2012; Constantinople and Bruno, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: At least 40% of somatic transients attenuate in a distance-dependent manner along the apical trunk and distal tufts.
source: While somato-dendritic coupling can be strong in L5 neurons (Beaulieu-Laroche et al., 2019), it is asymmetric; at least 40% of somatic transients attenuate in a distance-dependent manner along the apical trunk and distal tufts (Francioni et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The non-overlapping anatomical inputs and asymmetric coupling together could produce different learning-related effects on apical tuft and somatic stimulus representations.
source: The non-overlapping anatomical inputs and asymmetric coupling together could produce different learning-related effects on apical tuft and somatic stimulus representations.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the divergence from previous studies.

claim: Learning-related changes may manifest differently in layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal cells.
source: Second, learning-related changes may manifest differently in layer 2/3, the usual focus of previous studies (Poort et al., 2015; Henschke et al., 2020), and layer 5 pyramidal cells, the tufts of which we studied.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the divergence from previous studies.

claim: Most excitatory cells in layer 2/3 project to other cortical areas to affect further cortical processing.
source: With the exception of a small population of corticostriatal cells, most excitatory cells in layer 2/3 project to other cortical areas to affect further cortical processing (Petersen and Crochet, 2013; Yamashita et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Many L5 cells project to subcortical structures including the thalamus, superior colliculus, and brainstem, which may directly trigger behavioral responses.
source: In contrast, many L5 cells project to subcortical structures including the thalamus, superior colliculus, and brainstem, which may directly trigger behavioral responses (Llinás et al., 1998; Krauzlis et al., 2013; Parvizi and Damasio, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: In discrimination paradigms, both stimuli are relevant to behavior.
source: In discrimination paradigms, both stimuli are relevant to behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about discrimination tasks.

claim: An enhanced representation of both stimuli in layer 5 would be advantageous for animals to perform the task efficiently.
source: Thus, an enhanced representation of both stimuli in layer 5 would be advantageous for animals to perform the task efficiently.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance.

claim: Apical dendrite activation of subcortical-targeting pyramidal tract L5 cells, but not intratelencephalic L5 cells, determines the detection of tactile stimuli.
source: Recently, it was shown that apical dendrite activation of subcortical-targeting pyramidal tract L5 cells, but not intratelencephalic L5 cells that are more like L2/3 cells in their connectivity, determines the detection of tactile stimuli (Takahashi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Rbp4-Cre mice label a heterogenous population of layer 5 pyramidal cells, comprising both pyramidal tract and intratelencephalic neurons.
source: The Rbp4-Cre mice we used in this study labels a heterogenous population of layer 5 pyramidal cells, comprising both pyramidal tract and intratelencephalic neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the mouse line used in the study.

claim: Learning-related changes in sensory representations may manifest differently between a somatosensory modality and a visual modality.
source: Finally, it is possible that learning-related changes in sensory representations manifest differently between a somatosensory modality and a visual modality, the latter being the focus of previous studies.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the divergence from previous studies.

claim: This is the first study to show changes of sensory representations in somatosensory cortex within a discrimination paradigm.
source: To our knowledge, we are the first to show changes of sensory representations in somatosensory cortex within a discrimination paradigm.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Facial stimuli are generally more salient than arbitrary visual stimuli for any species.
source: Facial stimuli are generally more salient than arbitrary visual stimuli for any species, and mice are known to be highly responsive to their tactile sense more so than vision (Petty and Bruno, 2024).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by a citation.

claim: Mice are known to be highly responsive to their tactile sense more so than vision.
source: Facial stimuli are generally more salient than arbitrary visual stimuli for any species, and mice are known to be highly responsive to their tactile sense more so than vision (Petty and Bruno, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The strong salience of whisker-mediated touch may make it particularly advantageous to develop sensory representations of a larger variety of relevant tactile stimuli.
source: This strong salience of whisker-mediated touch may make it particularly advantageous to develop sensory representations of a larger variety of relevant tactile stimuli, in this case, both the CS+ and CS-.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why both stimuli are enhanced.

claim: Enhanced selectivity could be due to changes in local synaptic connectivity, long-range inputs, or both.
source: Enhanced selectivity could be due to changes in local synaptic connectivity, long-range inputs, or both.
evidence: This is a statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Learning may strengthen and weaken synapses onto barrel cortex neurons from ascending thalamocortical input or from neighboring cells.
source: Learning may strengthen and weaken synapses onto barrel cortex neurons from ascending thalamocortical input or from neighboring cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Other cortical regions encoding task context could via long-range inputs reconfigure barrel cortex to respond more strongly to these stimuli.
source: Alternatively or additionally, other cortical regions encoding task context could via long-range inputs reconfigure barrel cortex to respond more strongly to these stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: Enhanced representations persist after mice are no longer engaged in the task and receiving rewards, suggesting that enhanced representations may be a product of local plasticity in sensory cortex that alters receptive fields.
source: However, we found that enhanced representations persist after mice are no longer engaged in the task and receiving rewards. This result suggests that enhanced representations may be a product of local plasticity in sensory cortex that alters receptive fields.
evidence: This is an inference from the persistence of enhanced representations.

claim: Repeated exposure to stimuli can drive plasticity in sensory cortex and alter response tuning even in the absence of reward.
source: Even in the absence of reward, repeated exposure to stimuli can drive plasticity in sensory cortex and alter response tuning.
evidence: This is a general statement about plasticity.

claim: Repeated exposure to oriented gratings can alter the orientation tuning of cells in primary visual cortex.
source: For instance, repeated exposure to oriented gratings can alter the orientation tuning of cells in primary visual cortex (Yao and Dan, 2001; Dragoi et al., 2002; Dragoi et al., 2000), and overstimulation of whiskers induces plasticity at dendritic spines and alters whisker representations in somatosensory cortex (Zhang et al., 2015; Feldman and Brecht, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Overstimulation of whiskers induces plasticity at dendritic spines and alters whisker representations in somatosensory cortex.
source: For instance, repeated exposure to oriented gratings can alter the orientation tuning of cells in primary visual cortex (Yao and Dan, 2001; Dragoi et al., 2002; Dragoi et al., 2000), and overstimulation of whiskers induces plasticity at dendritic spines and alters whisker representations in somatosensory cortex (Zhang et al., 2015; Feldman and Brecht, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At the population level enhanced representations developed only when stimuli were behaviorally relevant.
source: Our results demonstrate that at the population level enhanced representations developed only when stimuli were behaviorally relevant.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding comparing conditioned and repeated exposure groups.

claim: While the response dynamics of some tufts changed after repeated stimuli presentations, overall selectivity of the population did not increase when rewards were omitted.
